abstract.t: This document defines the HTTP status code 430 (Consent Required). A server returns 430 when it declines a request because the usage the client declared, or that the server inferred, conflicts with a usage preference expressed for the requested content.

Mechanisms for expressing such preferences are defined elsewhere, notably by and . Those documents deliberately provide no enforcement mechanism. This document supplies one, without constraining how preferences are expressed or attached.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Machine-readable expressions of preference about how content may be used by automated systems are being standardised. defines a vocabulary for such preferences, and describes ways of attaching them to content. Both are explicit that they do not provide enforcement: "Enforcement is not provided by this specification. Preferences do not themselves create rights, obligations, or prohibitions."

That leaves a gap. A server that has published a preference, and that receives a request conflicting with it, has no status code whose semantics match what has happened. The existing codes each describe something else:

dl.dd: The server understood the request and refuses to authorise it. This invites the client to authenticate, which is not the remedy: the client is not unauthorised, it has declared a usage the origin has not consented to.
The request is missing a conditional header field. This is about request syntax, not about agreement.
Access is denied as a result of a legal demand. A usage preference is ordinarily not a legal demand, and conflating the two overstates the claim.

section.t: 430 (Consent Required) says something none of these say: the resource exists, the client may well be entitled to retrieve it, and the specific use it declared is one the origin has not consented to.

section.name: Conventions and Definitions
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.
The terms "usage preference", "usage category" and "asset" are used as defined in .

section.name: 430 Consent Required
section.t: The 430 (Consent Required) status code indicates that the server declines to fulfil the request because the usage associated with it conflicts with a usage preference expressed for the target resource.
A server MAY return 430 when both of the following hold:

ul.li: a usage preference applying to the target resource disallows a usage category, by any mechanism including those in ; and
the server determines that the request is associated with that usage category, whether from a usage declaration made by the client or by other means.

section.t: A server MUST NOT return 430 solely because a request originates from an automated client. The status code reports a conflict with a declared preference, not the identity or nature of the requester.

A server that returns 430 SHOULD include a representation explaining which usage category was refused, so that a client can distinguish a refused usage from a malformed request. A server MUST NOT include in that explanation any information it would not disclose to an unauthenticated client.

A response carrying 430 SHOULD include a Link header field whose relation type is "usage-preferences" and whose target identifies the preference expression the server applied. This allows a client to retrieve the preference and determine whether a compliant request is possible.
A 430 response is heuristically cacheable by default, as described in . A server SHOULD send explicit cache directives where the preference is expected to change.
Because a preference is not an authorisation decision, a client SHOULD NOT retry a 430 response with credentials. A client MAY retry if it can declare a usage that the preference permits.

section.name: Example
section.t: A client declares a training usage for a resource whose origin has expressed a preference disallowing that category:
section.sourcecode: GET /article HTTP/1.1 Host: example.org Content-Usage: train-ai=n
section.t: The origin declines:
section.sourcecode:
HTTP/1.1 430 Consent Required Content-Type: application/json Link: <https://example.org/.well-known/aibdp.json>; rel="usage-preferences" Content-Usage: train-ai=n
{ "refused-category": "train-ai", "preferences": "https://example.org/.well-known/aibdp.json" }
section.t: The representation format shown is illustrative; this document does not define one.

section.name: Relationship to Preference Expression
section.t: This document is deliberately independent of how preferences are expressed or attached. It applies equally to preferences conveyed by the Content-Usage header field or the robots.txt rule of , and to richer declaration formats such as , which expresses conditional permissions and per-path scope that the base vocabulary does not.

Where a declaration format distinguishes a conditional permission from a refusal, a server SHOULD return 430 for a request that does not satisfy the stated conditions, and SHOULD indicate the unmet conditions in the response.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: 430 reports the outcome of applying a published preference. It therefore discloses only information the origin has already published, and servers MUST NOT use the explanation permitted in to disclose more.
A server that returns 430 discloses that a preference applies to the resource. Where the existence of a preference is itself sensitive, a server SHOULD return 404 or 403 as appropriate instead.

Neither this status code nor the preferences it enforces are authenticated. A client can disregard a 430 response, and a server can return 430 without any preference having been published. Deployments requiring assurance beyond a cooperating client's good faith need mechanisms outside the scope of this document.
Because 430 responses may be cached, a server that changes a preference SHOULD invalidate affected responses; a stale 430 refuses a usage the origin now permits.
